{{< include _compose-kit.qmd >}}

A melody is a line of notes that a listener can follow and remember. Most melodies that work have a few things in common.
This lesson takes them one at a time, with a short example of each you can play. At the end you write eight bars of your own.

**How to use the page.** Press ▶ under any staff to hear it on the piano. The note that is sounding turns red.

## 1. Shape: where the line goes

Draw a melody as a line on paper, going up and down with the pitch, and you get its **contour**. A
good melody usually has one clear shape: an arch (up, then down), a wave, or a long fall. Most of it moves
by **step** (to the next note of the scale), with a few **leaps**. After a big leap, the line usually turns and steps back the other way:
that fills the gap the leap left.

::: {.ax-pair}
<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="96"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:An arch: steps, one leap, a peak, then down
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C2 D2 E2 G2 | A2 G2 c4 | B2 A2 G2 F2 | E2 D2 C4 |]
</script></div>

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="96"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:No shape: leaps everywhere, no peak
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
C2 A2 D2 B2 | E2 c2 F2 G,2 | B,2 A2 C2 a2 | D6 z2 |]
</script></div>
:::

The first has a **climax**: one highest note (the high C), reached once, on a strong beat, by a leap, and left by steps going down.
The second leaps up and down at random. It is hard to sing back and hard to remember.

<div class="cp-tip">
<strong>Rule of thumb.</strong> One high point, reached once. Mostly steps. Leap to a strong note, then step back. Keep it inside about an octave
unless you have a reason not to.
</div>

## 2. Rhythm that comes back

A listener remembers rhythm before pitch. If the opening rhythm comes back, the melody holds together even when the notes change.
Here the same rhythm (two eighths and a quarter, twice) is used in three bars out of four, with new notes each time:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="100"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:One rhythm, three times, then a long note
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:G
GA B2 GA B2 | AB c2 AB c2 | Bc d2 cB A2 | G8 |]
</script></div>

Try it the other way too: keep the notes and change the rhythm. Both are ways of **developing** an idea, which is the subject of
[Composing 2](compose-motif.qmd).

## 3. Phrases: question and answer

Melodies come in **phrases**, usually four bars long, ending with a **cadence**: a resting point, like a comma or a full stop
(see [Cadences](cadences.qmd)). Two phrases often pair up as a question and an answer.

### The period

A **period** is eight bars: two four-bar phrases that start the same way. The first, the **antecedent**, ends with a weak cadence, often on
the dominant (a half cadence). The second, the **consequent**, starts like the first and ends with a strong cadence on the tonic.
It sounds like a question and its answer.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="104" data-width="680"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:A period in C: bars 1-4 ask, bars 5-8 answer
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:C
"C"E2 G2 c2 G2 | "F"A2 F2 "C"G4 | "F"A2 c2 "C"G2 E2 | "G"D6 z2 |
"C"E2 G2 c2 G2 | "F"A2 F2 "C"G4 | "F"A2 F2 "G7"D2 B,2 | "C"C6 z2 |]
</script></div>

Bars 5–6 copy bars 1–2. Bar 4 stops on D over G: it wants to go on. Bar 8 lands on C over C: it is finished.

### The sentence

A **sentence** is also eight bars, but it is built differently. A short **basic idea** (two bars) is stated and repeated
(bars 1–4, the **presentation**). Then the **continuation** speeds up: the idea breaks into smaller pieces, and it drives to a cadence (bars 5–8).

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="104" data-width="680"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:A sentence in D: idea, idea again, pieces, cadence
M:4/4
L:1/8
K:D
"D"D2 F2 A4 | "D"F2 E2 D4 | "A"E2 G2 B4 | "A"G2 F2 E4 |
"D"FG A2 "G"GA B2 | "D"AB c2 "Bm"Bc d2 | "G"B2 "A7"A2 G2 E2 | "D"D8 |]
</script></div>

Bars 3–4 repeat bars 1–2 a step higher. In bars 5–6 the two-bar idea is cut down to two-beat pieces, which makes the music speed up.

<div class="cp-tip">
<strong>Which plan?</strong> A period sounds balanced and song-like: it suits a tune people will sing back. A sentence sounds like it is
going somewhere: it suits a theme that has to build. Both are eight bars; both end on the tonic.
</div>

## 4. Fitting the chords

If the melody has chords under it, the notes on strong beats (beats 1 and 3 in 4/4) usually belong to the chord. Notes between them can be
anything that steps: they pass through or turn round and come back. In the period above, every note on beat 1 is in the chord written over it.
[Guide tones](guide-tones.qmd) and [reharmonizing](reharmonize.qmd) go further.

## 5. Write eight bars

Open the [Notation page](/tools/notation.qmd) and write a period or a sentence, in any key you can play.
A checklist to read before you start and again when you finish:

1. Does it have one high point? Where is it?
2. Is it mostly steps? Does each big leap turn back?
3. Does a rhythm come back?
4. Does bar 4 end open (not on the tonic), and bar 8 closed (on the tonic, on a strong beat)?
5. Can you sing it back without looking?

Keep **every version** you write, not only the last one, and note what you changed and why. That is the evidence that shows how
you developed the piece: see [Process 1: Keeping a Process Journal](process-journal.qmd).

Next: [Composing 2: Developing a Motif](compose-motif.qmd).
